goods.source: UN Comtrade, annual, HS, goods exports to World

services.source: World Bank WDI, from IMF balance-of-payments returns

notes.CIV: The cocoa superpower: roughly 2 million tonnes a year from about a million smallholdings, most of them under five hectares.
notes.GHA: Sells through COCOBOD, a state board that fixes a farmgate price. A failed 2023 harvest and heavy smuggling into neighbouring countries pushed Ghana behind Ecuador for the first time.
notes.ECU: The fastest-growing origin in the world and the home of fine-flavour Nacional cacao. It now out-exports every Asian producer.
notes.NGA: Cocoa was Nigeria’s largest export before oil was found; the sector is being revived to diversify away from crude.
notes.CMR: Distinctive dark-red beans, shipped largely through the port of Douala.
notes.NLD: Amsterdam is the largest cocoa port on earth. The Netherlands grinds and re-exports beans it does not grow.
notes.BEL: Antwerp storage and Belgian grinding capacity. The chocolate reputation sits downstream of the trade, not the farming.
notes.PER: A leading organic and fine-flavour origin, much of it planted as an alternative to coca.
notes.DOM: The world’s largest exporter of certified organic cocoa.
notes.IDN: Once the world’s number three. Export taxes pushed the crop into domestic grinding rather than raw bean exports.
notes.BRA: A major grower that eats almost its entire crop.
notes.VEN: Home of Criollo, the rarest and most prized cacao variety.
notes.MEX: Where cacao was first domesticated and drunk, several thousand years ago.

notes.BRA: About a third of all the coffee grown on earth. A single frost in Minas Gerais moves the global price.
notes.CHE: Grows no coffee whatsoever. Switzerland is the world’s number two exporter by value because of capsules — coffee leaves the country worth more per kilo than most of what else does.
notes.COL: The benchmark for washed arabica. The growers’ federation represents roughly 540,000 farming families.
notes.VNM: Built the modern robusta market from almost nothing after 1986. Most instant coffee starts here.
notes.DEU: Hamburg is Europe’s coffee port; Germany roasts and re-exports across the EU.
notes.ITA: Espresso as an export industry — roasted blends, and the machines to make them.
notes.ETH: The botanical birthplace of arabica and the only country with wild coffee forests.
notes.IDN: Sumatran robusta plus the specialty Sulawesi and Java crops.
notes.HND: Central America’s largest producer, having overtaken Guatemala over the last decade.
notes.UGA: Coffee is Uganda’s single biggest export earner.
notes.PER: The largest exporter of organic coffee in the world.
notes.IND: Almost all of it grown in shade, under a forest canopy.
notes.KEN: Small volumes, but Kenyan AA fetches some of the highest auction prices anywhere.
notes.CHN: Yunnan has quietly become a serious arabica origin.
Where tea comes from, and still the largest exporter by value — overwhelmingly green tea.
notes.LKA: Ceylon tea: about a sixth of the world’s tea exports by value, from an island the size of Ireland.
notes.KEN: The largest black tea exporter in the world, mostly CTC leaf bound for teabags in Pakistan, Egypt and Britain.
notes.IND: Assam and Darjeeling are famous, but India drinks around 80% of what it grows.
notes.ARE: Dubai has built a tea blending and re-export hub with no plantations of its own.
notes.POL: A packaging and re-export centre for the EU market.
notes.JPN: Small volumes at very high prices — matcha and sencha.
notes.GBR: Blends and re-exports; the classic tea nation that grows none.
notes.ARG: Bulk low-cost leaf, most of it destined for American iced tea.
notes.MWI: The first country in Africa to grow tea commercially.
notes.TWN: Oolong, sold at some of the highest prices per kilo in the trade.

notes.SAU: The swing producer: the only country holding meaningful spare capacity, which is what lets OPEC+ move prices at all.
notes.RUS: Since 2022 the barrels have not stopped, they have changed address — Europe out, India and China in, at a discount.
notes.USA: A net crude exporter only since the 2015 repeal of the export ban, on the back of shale. Now the largest producer in the world.
notes.CAN: Alberta oil sands, sold almost entirely to a single customer: the United States.
notes.ARE: Murban crude now trades on its own futures exchange in Abu Dhabi.
notes.IRQ: Oil funds roughly 90% of the Iraqi state budget.
notes.NOR: Revenues feed the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, worth well over a trillion dollars.
notes.NGA: Africa’s biggest producer, long hampered by theft and pipeline sabotage in the Niger Delta.
notes.KAZ: Landlocked — most of its crude reaches the sea through a single pipeline across Russia.
notes.BRA: Pre-salt fields off Rio have made Brazil one of the fastest-growing exporters of the decade.
notes.IRN: Sanctioned; real volumes are opaque and move mostly to China.
notes.GUY: Had no oil industry at all before 2019 and is now among the fastest-growing economies on earth.
notes.VEN: Sits on the largest proven reserves in the world and exports a fraction of what it once did.
notes.ARG: Vaca Muerta shale is turning a net importer back into an exporter.
notes.SSD: Depends on a pipeline through Sudan to reach any market at all.

notes.USA: From zero LNG exports in 2015 to the world’s largest, almost entirely from Gulf Coast terminals fed by shale.
notes.QAT: The North Field is the largest gas field on earth, shared with Iran. Qatar is expanding capacity by about 85% this decade.
notes.AUS: Briefly the world’s top LNG exporter; ships mostly to Japan, China and South Korea.
notes.RUS: Pipeline exports to Europe collapsed after 2022. Power of Siberia to China absorbs only a fraction of the lost volume.
notes.NOR: Became Europe’s single largest gas supplier almost overnight when Russian flows stopped.
notes.NLD: A trading hub rather than a producer now — the giant Groningen field was shut for good in 2024 after years of earthquakes.
notes.DZA: Supplies Italy and Spain through undersea pipelines across the Mediterranean.
notes.TKM: Enormous reserves and effectively one customer: China.
notes.BEL: Zeebrugge is a major LNG re-loading point for the EU.
notes.TTO: One of the earliest LNG exporters to the United States. That trade has since reversed.
notes.MOZ: Vast offshore fields whose development has been repeatedly halted by an insurgency in Cabo Delgado.

notes.TWN: TSMC alone accounts for the great majority of leading-edge foundry capacity worldwide. At the smallest node sizes there is no substitute.
notes.HKG: Almost pure transit — chips moving between mainland Chinese factories and everyone else.
notes.CHN: By far the largest importer of chips, and a large exporter too: mostly assembly, packaging and re-export rather than fabrication.
notes.KOR: Samsung and SK Hynix dominate memory, which is far more cyclical than logic.
notes.SGP: Both a real fab cluster and a trans-shipment hub for the region.
notes.MYS: Penang has been the world’s back-end assembly and test hub since the 1970s — roughly a tenth of global packaging.
notes.USA: Designs far more than it makes. The CHIPS Act is an attempt to close that gap.
notes.JPN: Lost the chip crown in the 1990s but still supplies critical materials, wafers and equipment.
notes.VNM: The fastest-growing assembly base as firms diversify away from China.
notes.DEU: Dresden is Europe’s largest chip cluster; Infineon leads in automotive power semiconductors.
notes.PHL: A long-established assembly and test location.
notes.NLD: ASML in Veldhoven is the only company on earth that makes EUV lithography machines.
notes.ISR: Intel’s largest fabs outside the United States.
notes.IND: A huge chip design workforce; its first large fabs are only now being built.

notes.DEU: The highest value per car of any large exporter. The premium segment is essentially a German industry.
notes.JPN: Held the volume crown for most of the last fifty years and lost it to China in 2023.
notes.CHN: Overtook Japan on units in 2023. BYD outsold Tesla on battery EVs the same year.
notes.MEX: Built to supply the US market under NAFTA and now USMCA. More cars leave Mexico than Spain or Korea.
notes.KOR: Hyundai and Kia went from budget brands to the third-largest carmaking group in the world.
notes.ESP: Europe’s second-largest producer, almost entirely in foreign-owned plants.
notes.BEL: Zeebrugge and Antwerp are the biggest vehicle ports in the world. Most of these cars are simply passing through.
notes.GBR: Volumes are well down since 2016, but the mix is unusually premium — JLR, Bentley, Rolls-Royce, Mini.
notes.CZE: Škoda plus Hyundai and Toyota plants. Cars are around a fifth of all Czech exports.
notes.SVK: Builds more cars per head of population than any other country on earth.
notes.THA: The "Detroit of Asia" — the assembly base for Japanese makers across Southeast Asia.
notes.ZAF: BMW, Mercedes and VW plants exporting into Europe.
notes.ROU: Dacia — the budget brand that became Renault’s profit engine.
notes.MAR: Tangier has grown into one of Africa’s largest industrial export hubs.

notes.FRA: Champagne and Bordeaux alone out-earn most countries’ entire wine industries.
notes.ITA: The largest exporter by volume. Prosecco drove most of the growth of the last fifteen years.
notes.ESP: Ships more litres than France at roughly a fifth of the price per litre — much of it moves in bulk.
notes.CHL: Built on ungrafted vines that survived phylloxera behind the shield of the Andes and the Atacama.
notes.AUS: Lost its largest market almost overnight when China imposed tariffs in 2020. They were lifted in 2024.
notes.NZL: One grape, one region: Marlborough sauvignon blanc is most of this number.
notes.USA: California is the fourth-largest wine producer on earth but drinks most of what it makes.
notes.PRT: Port and Douro reds — and the world’s dominant cork industry alongside.
notes.ARG: Malbec, a grape that nearly died out in France and was reborn in Mendoza.
notes.GBR: Re-exports. London has been a wine trading centre for centuries.
notes.ZAF: Stellenbosch and the Cape, where wine has been made since the 1650s.
notes.HKG: A duty-free auction and re-export hub for fine wine into Asia.
notes.GEO: The oldest continuous winemaking tradition known — roughly 8,000 years, still using buried clay qvevri.
notes.MDA: Wine is a larger share of national exports here than almost anywhere else.

notes.DEU: Europe’s largest pharma exporter. BioNTech’s mRNA vaccine alone moved the national trade balance in 2021.
notes.CHE: Roche and Novartis. Pharma is around 40% of everything Switzerland exports.
notes.IRL: Pharma and chemicals are over half of Irish goods exports — a consequence of corporate tax structuring as much as of factories.
notes.BEL: A distribution and repackaging hub for the EU, on a scale far beyond its own consumption.
notes.DNK: Novo Nordisk’s GLP-1 drugs have grown so fast that Danish GDP is now discussed with and without them.
notes.IND: The "pharmacy of the world" — a large share of global generic volume, a small share of global value.
notes.SVN: A tiny country with a serious generics industry — Lek and Krka.
notes.HUN: Gedeon Richter, one of the oldest pharmaceutical companies in continental Europe.
notes.ISR: Teva is the largest generic drugmaker in the world.

notes.CHE: Four refineries, in a country with no gold mines, process a large share of all the gold produced on earth each year.
notes.GBR: London vaults set the benchmark price twice a day. The bars themselves rarely move far.
notes.ARE: Dubai’s gold souk and free zone — and a persistent route for artisanal African gold.
notes.HKG: The traditional gateway into mainland Chinese demand.
notes.AUS: A genuine mining exporter, and the second-largest producer in the world.
notes.CAN: Toronto is also where most of the world’s mining companies are listed.
notes.ZAF: Produced most of the world’s gold for a century. Its mines are now the deepest anywhere, and among the most depleted.
notes.GHA: Africa’s largest producer — the country the British named the Gold Coast.
notes.MLI: Gold is roughly three-quarters of everything Mali exports.
notes.RUS: Was around $18bn before 2022; G7 import bans pushed the trade towards China and the UAE.
notes.IDN: Grasberg in Papua is one of the largest gold and copper deposits ever found.
notes.ITA: Vicenza and Arezzo — jewellery manufacturing at industrial scale.
notes.COD: Much of it artisanal, and much of it smuggled out through neighbouring countries.

notes.RUS: Roughly a fifth of world exports and rising. Two decades ago Russia was a net importer.
notes.AUS: Volumes swing wildly with drought — a bad year can halve the crop.
notes.USA: Once the dominant exporter; its share has fallen steadily as Russia and the Black Sea scaled up.
notes.CAN: High-protein spring wheat, the milling benchmark for bread flour.
notes.FRA: The EU’s largest producer, a traditional supplier to Algeria and Morocco.
notes.UKR: Exports survived the 2022 invasion only through a grain corridor and Danube barges.
notes.ROU: Constanța on the Black Sea became a critical outlet for Ukrainian grain as well as Romanian.
notes.IND: The second-largest producer in the world, but it banned exports in 2022 to protect domestic supply.
notes.TUR: Imports grain, mills it, and exports flour — the largest flour exporter in the world.

notes.IND: About 40% of all rice traded globally by volume, and a third by value. Restrictions on non-basmati exports in 2023 sent world prices to a 15-year high.
notes.THA: The premium end: jasmine rice, and the long-time benchmark for world pricing.
notes.VNM: The Mekong Delta, one of the most productive rice landscapes on earth — and one of the most exposed to salt intrusion.
notes.PAK: Basmati, sold mainly into the Gulf and East Africa.
notes.USA: Arkansas and the Mississippi delta; mostly long-grain, sold to Latin America and Japan.
notes.ITA: Europe’s rice bowl is the Po valley — arborio and carnaroli for risotto.
notes.KHM: Fragrant rice that has repeatedly won international taste competitions.
notes.CHN: A huge producer that is a net importer in most years.
notes.URY: Small country, unusually high yields, almost all of the crop exported.

notes.IDN: Over half of world supply. Jakarta has twice halted exports outright to hold down domestic cooking oil prices.
notes.MYS: The original commercial producer, and still the source of most industry standards and certification.
notes.NLD: Rotterdam refines and re-exports; almost all EU palm oil lands here first.
notes.GTM: The highest yields per hectare in the world, above even Indonesia.
notes.COL: The largest producer in the Americas.
notes.SGP: Head office rather than plantation: the largest palm oil trading houses are Singapore-listed.
notes.IND: Imports crude palm oil, refines it and re-exports some of the product.
notes.NGA: Once the world’s leading exporter, before Southeast Asia took over in the 1960s.

notes.ECU: A quarter of world exports, and the only major exporter where most plantations are locally owned rather than run by multinationals.
notes.PHL: Supplies Japan, Korea and China; hit hard by the latest Panama disease outbreak.
notes.CRI: The original "banana republic" economy, and still among the most productive.
notes.NLD: Rotterdam is Europe’s banana gateway. None of these were grown in the Netherlands.
notes.BEL: Antwerp handles a large share of Europe’s fruit imports and re-exports.
notes.DOM: The largest exporter of organic bananas in the world.
notes.PER: A specialist organic and fair-trade origin.
notes.IND: The largest banana producer on earth by a wide margin — and it eats nearly all of them.

notes.CHN: Both the largest producer and the world’s processing floor — much of the whitefish caught in the North Pacific is filleted here and re-exported.
notes.NOR: Atlantic salmon, farmed in the fjords, is one of the great export successes of the last forty years.
notes.VNM: Pangasius and shrimp from the Mekong Delta.
notes.CHL: The world’s number two salmon farmer, in fjords on the other side of the planet from Norway.
notes.ECU: Farmed shrimp exports have roughly quadrupled in a decade and now rival bananas as an earner.
notes.IND: Vannamei shrimp, sold mainly to the United States.
notes.USA: Alaska pollock, salmon and crab — much of it exported for processing and then re-imported.
notes.RUS: Pollock and crab from the Sea of Okhotsk.
notes.CAN: Lobster is the single most valuable seafood export.
notes.ESP: Europe’s largest fishing fleet and its biggest seafood consumer per head.
notes.SWE: Mostly Norwegian salmon crossing the border, processed and sent on.
notes.THA: The historic centre of the canned tuna industry.
notes.PER: Anchoveta — the largest single-species fishery in the world, almost all of it turned into fishmeal.
notes.POL: A major processor of imported salmon and herring for the EU market.
notes.MAR: Africa’s largest seafood exporter, built on sardines and octopus.
notes.ISL: Fish is around 40% of Icelandic goods exports.
notes.FRO: The Faroe Islands: 50,000 people, and one of the largest seafood exporters per head on earth.

notes.IND: Surat cuts and polishes the overwhelming majority of the world’s diamonds — an industry of around a million workers.
notes.ARE: Dubai has overtaken Antwerp as the largest rough diamond trading centre in the world.
notes.BEL: Antwerp ran the global diamond trade for five centuries and still handles an enormous share of it.
notes.HKG: The route into Chinese jewellery demand.
notes.ISR: Ramat Gan, historically the centre for larger, higher-value polished stones.
notes.USA: The largest consumer market in the world, and a substantial re-exporter.
notes.BWA: The mining success story: diamond revenue took Botswana from one of the poorest countries at independence to middle income.
notes.RUS: Alrosa produces roughly a third of the world’s rough by volume; G7 sanctions since 2024 have complicated every step of the chain.
notes.ZAF: Where the modern industry began, at Kimberley in the 1870s.
notes.CAN: Arctic mines opened in the 1990s, marketed hard on ethical provenance.
notes.NAM: Unusually, much of it dredged from the seabed off the Atlantic coast.
notes.LSO: A tiny mountain kingdom that produces an outsized number of very large stones.
notes.COD: High volume, low value — mostly industrial-grade stones.
notes.AUS: The Argyle mine, source of most of the world’s pink diamonds, closed in 2020.
notes.THA: A major cutting and jewellery-setting centre.

notes.CHL: Around a quarter of world supply. Copper is roughly half of everything Chile exports, and state-owned Codelco is the largest producer on earth.
notes.PER: The second-largest producer; mining conflicts with Andean communities regularly close roads and mines.
notes.COD: The fastest-growing major producer, and the world’s dominant cobalt source alongside it.
notes.IDN: Now bans raw ore exports outright to force smelting to happen domestically.
notes.ZMB: The other half of the Copperbelt, and the country’s overwhelming export earner.
notes.JPN: Imports ore, smelts it, exports refined metal. Almost no copper is mined in Japan.
notes.POL: KGHM works one of the largest underground copper deposits in the world, in Lower Silesia.
notes.MNG: Oyu Tolgoi is so large that its output measurably moves Mongolian GDP.

notes.CHN: Over half of world exports, and a far larger share of the cathode, anode and refining steps upstream of the cell.
notes.KOR: LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On — the main non-Chinese alternative at scale.
notes.POL: LG’s Wrocław plant is the largest battery factory in Europe, and batteries are now a top Polish export.
notes.HUN: Samsung SDI at Göd and a very large CATL plant under construction at Debrecen.
notes.JPN: Invented the commercial lithium-ion cell in 1991 and has steadily lost share since.
notes.SWE: Northvolt was Europe’s attempt at a home-grown champion; its 2024 collapse reset those ambitions.

notes.CHN: Still roughly a third of world exports, though its share has been falling for a decade as costs rise.
notes.BGD: Clothing is over 80% of everything Bangladesh exports — the highest dependence on a single sector of any large economy.
notes.VNM: The main beneficiary of manufacturers diversifying away from China.
notes.ITA: The luxury end. Italy exports a fraction of China’s volume at many times the price per garment.
notes.DEU: Mostly a logistics and re-export role for the EU market.
notes.TUR: Close enough to Europe to restock in days rather than weeks — the fast fashion advantage.
notes.ESP: Inditex — Zara’s parent — is headquartered in Galicia and routes a large share of its stock through Spain.
notes.PAK: Unusually, an integrated industry — Pakistan grows its own cotton, spins it and sews it.
notes.PRT: Europe’s quality knitwear base, and increasingly a near-shoring destination.
notes.LKA: Specialises in technical sportswear and lingerie rather than basics.
notes.ETH: A state push to build a garment industry, slowed sharply by the Tigray conflict and the loss of duty-free US access.

notes.NLD: Royal FloraHolland in Aalsmeer is the largest flower auction on earth, in one of the largest buildings on earth. Much of what it sells was grown in Africa that week.
notes.COL: Supplies most of the flowers Americans buy, especially the enormous Valentine’s Day peak.
notes.ECU: Equatorial light and 2,800m altitude give Ecuadorian roses unusually large heads and long stems.
notes.KEN: Grown around Lake Naivasha and flown out overnight — flowers are one of Kenya’s top export earners.
notes.ETH: A deliberate state-backed industry, built from scratch in about twenty years.
notes.CHN: Yunnan supplies most of Asia, through the Kunming auction market.
notes.ISR: The country that pioneered the airfreight flower model in the 1970s.

notes.DEU: Europe's confectionery factory, and the single largest exporter of chocolate in the world — from a country that cannot grow a cocoa tree.
notes.BEL: The praline was invented in Brussels in 1912. Belgian chocolate is a protected quality standard as much as a place of origin.
notes.ITA: Ferrero — Nutella, Kinder and Rocher — is one of the largest confectionery companies on earth and privately held.
notes.POL: The fastest-growing manufacturing base in the EU for chocolate, on lower costs than the west of the union.
notes.NLD: Amsterdam grinds the beans; the Netherlands then sells both the cocoa butter and the finished bars.
notes.CHE: Invented milk chocolate and conching, and still commands the highest price per kilo of any large exporter.
notes.CIV: Grows more cocoa than any other country and barely registers on this map. That gap is the whole point of putting the two side by side.
notes.CAN: A large exporter almost entirely because of proximity to the United States.
notes.TUR: Built a serious confectionery export industry aimed at the Middle East and Central Asia.
notes.MEX: Where chocolate was first drunk, several thousand years before Europe had heard of it.

notes.BRA: Overtook the United States in 2013 and has widened the lead every year since. The Cerrado savanna was made farmable by soil science in the 1970s, and it is now the largest soy region on earth.
notes.USA: The Midwest crop was built around Chinese demand. When Beijing put tariffs on it in 2018, exports fell by roughly half in a season.
notes.PRY: Landlocked, and ships almost everything down the Paraná river on barges — the level of that river is a national economic variable.
notes.ARG: Exports far more soy meal and oil than beans: a deliberately tiered export tax pushes the crop into domestic crushing plants first.
notes.URY: A very high share of the crop is exported — the domestic market is tiny.
notes.CAN: Non-GM identity-preserved beans for the Japanese tofu and miso market, sold at a premium.
notes.UKR: Sunflower is the bigger crop, but soy exports survived the war through the Danube ports.

notes.BRA: The largest exporter in the world, though by value Brazil, the United States and Australia are within a few points of each other. Cattle ranching is the largest single driver of Amazon deforestation, which is why EU deforestation rules land hardest here.
notes.USA: Exports high-value cuts to Japan and Korea while importing lean trimmings to mix into hamburger. The same country is a top-five exporter and a top-five importer.
notes.AUS: Herd numbers swing with drought on a multi-year cycle, and the export figure swings with them.
notes.IND: Almost entirely water buffalo, sold to Vietnam, Malaysia and Egypt. Slaughter of cattle proper is restricted or banned across most states.
notes.ARG: The classic beef nation, held back for decades by export bans and quotas imposed to keep domestic steak cheap.
notes.NLD: A processing and re-export hub for the EU rather than a cattle country.
notes.IRL: Grass-fed year round, and more beef is exported than eaten — the domestic market is far too small.
notes.NZL: Mostly lean manufacturing beef, a by-product of the dairy herd, sold into the American burger trade.
notes.URY: Every animal in the country is individually tagged and traceable, which is what opens the premium markets.
notes.POL: The EU's fastest-growing beef exporter, on low costs.

notes.DEU: The largest exporter by volume, and most of it is commodity gouda and mozzarella rather than anything with a protected name.
notes.NLD: Gouda and Edam, sold through a co-operative structure that has organised Dutch dairy for over a century.
notes.ITA: Parmigiano Reggiano and Grana Padano are protected designations with consortium-controlled production — and the highest price per kilo in the trade.
notes.FRA: Around 1,200 recognised varieties, some 50 of them with protected origin status.
notes.NZL: Fonterra collects nearly all of New Zealand's milk and is one of the largest dairy exporters in the world, shipping to Asia from the far side of the planet.
notes.DNK: Feta, oddly — Danish producers fought and lost a long EU case over the name, and now sell it outside Europe.
notes.IRL: Cheddar, historically almost all of it to Britain, which made Brexit an unusually specific problem.
notes.USA: Wisconsin and California; exports have grown fast on Mexican and Asian demand.
notes.POL: A large low-cost supplier to the rest of the EU.
notes.BLR: Belarus supplies Russia, which is why almost none of this shows up in EU statistics.

notes.BRA: Mills switch between sugar and ethanol week to week. No other agricultural producer has that kind of optionality over its own output.
notes.IND: The largest producer in the world in some years, and an unpredictable exporter: New Delhi restricts shipments whenever domestic prices rise.
notes.THA: Long the number two exporter, though drought and a shift to cassava have cut the crop.
notes.AUS: Queensland cane, almost all of it exported raw to refineries in Asia.
notes.GTM: The most efficient cane producer in the Americas after Brazil.
notes.FRA: Beet sugar. The EU abolished its production quotas in 2017 and European exports jumped.
notes.ARE: Al Khaleej in Dubai is one of the largest standalone refineries anywhere, importing raw sugar and selling it on refined.
notes.MEX: Sells into a US market whose sugar imports are governed by a bilateral agreement rather than the open market.

notes.ESP: Andalusia, and the province of Jaén alone has more olive trees than most countries have of anything. Two bad harvests in a row emptied world stocks.
notes.ITA: Both a producer and a hub: Italy imports Spanish and Tunisian oil in bulk, bottles it, and sells it on at a considerable premium.
notes.GRC: The highest olive oil consumption per head in the world, which leaves proportionally less to export.
notes.TUN: The largest producer outside the EU, selling mostly in bulk to Italian and Spanish bottlers rather than under its own name.
notes.PRT: The fastest-growing producer in Europe, on intensive hedge-planted groves.
notes.TUR: Alternates between exporting freely and banning bulk exports to hold down domestic prices.
notes.MAR: Production has been repeatedly cut by drought, turning an exporter into an occasional importer.

notes.GBR: Scotch whisky is the single largest food and drink export the United Kingdom has, and it is most of this figure.
notes.FRA: Cognac and armagnac. A slow year in China or the United States moves the whole national number.
notes.MEX: Tequila and mezcal can legally be made only in designated Mexican states. American demand has tripled exports in a decade.
notes.SGP: A duty-free re-export hub for spirits moving into Asia, distilling essentially none of it.
notes.USA: Bourbon, which by law must be made in the United States — and which the EU targeted with retaliatory tariffs in 2018.
notes.IRL: Irish whiskey was down to two working distilleries in 1980. It is now the fastest-growing whiskey category in the world.
notes.ITA: Aperitifs and grappa; the Aperol and Campari boom is visible in this line.
notes.SWE: Essentially one brand, Absolut, all of it distilled in a single town in Skåne.
notes.NLD: Genever, vodka and a large blending and bottling trade.
notes.DEU: A blending and re-export role more than a distilling one.

notes.USA: The Corn Belt grows more maize than any country on earth, and sends roughly a third of it to ethanol distilleries rather than to food or export.
notes.BRA: The safrinha — a second maize crop planted on the same land right after the soybeans come off — turned Brazil into a top exporter in about fifteen years.
notes.ARG: A major exporter despite years of export taxes and quotas intended to keep domestic food cheap.
notes.UKR: Maize is Ukraine's largest agricultural export by value, and it has to leave through Black Sea ports or Danube barges.
notes.FRA: The EU's biggest producer, though irrigation restrictions in dry summers now cap the crop.
notes.ZAF: White maize is the staple food of southern Africa, and South Africa is the region's supplier of last resort in a drought.
notes.HUN: One of the few EU members that consistently exports more grain than it eats.
notes.ROU: Constanța gives Romania the Black Sea outlet that its landlocked neighbours lack.

notes.BRA: A net importer within living memory, and now a close second on the scale and yields of Mato Grosso. Brazil passed the United States on volume in the 2023/24 season, though not yet on value.
notes.USA: The dominant exporter for most of the last century. American cotton subsidies have been contested at the WTO by West African growers for over twenty years.
notes.AUS: Irrigated cotton in New South Wales. Output tracks the water in the Murray-Darling and can fall by 90% in a drought.
notes.GRC: The European Union's only cotton grower of any size.
notes.BEN: Cotton is roughly three-quarters of everything Benin sells abroad — about as concentrated as a national export base gets.
notes.MLI: Africa's largest producer in a good year, and the crop that most of the rural south depends on.
notes.BFA: Grown by hundreds of thousands of smallholders; the crop collapsed and recovered over the GM cotton dispute of the 2010s.
notes.CIV: Cotton in the north, cocoa in the south — two entirely separate export economies in one country.
notes.TUR: Both a large grower and a large importer, because its own spinning mills consume more than it can plant.
notes.UZB: Stopped exporting raw cotton almost entirely, choosing to spin and sew it at home instead — a deliberate move up the chain.
notes.EGY: Extra-long staple cotton. The name is used on far more fabric worldwide than Egypt could possibly grow.

notes.USA: The Gulf Coast refining complex is the largest concentration of refining capacity in the world, and the US exports more fuel than any other country.
notes.RUS: Sanctions capped the price of Russian diesel and fuel oil rather than the volume, and the barrels found new buyers.
notes.IND: Jamnagar is the largest single refinery on earth. India bought heavily discounted Russian crude and sold the refined products onward, including to Europe.
notes.NLD: Rotterdam is Europe's refining and blending hub — crude in, diesel and gasoline out, almost none of it Dutch oil.
notes.SGP: Jurong Island refines for the whole region. Singapore has no oil of its own and refining is one of its largest industries.
notes.KOR: Four very large refineries built to run on imported Middle Eastern crude and export the products.
notes.SAU: Increasingly sells refined products rather than crude — the same barrel, worth more.
notes.ARE: Ruwais, plus a large fuel-blending and bunkering trade out of Fujairah.
notes.BEL: Antwerp, the second petrochemical cluster of northwest Europe after Rotterdam.

notes.AUS: Metallurgical coal for blast furnaces — the part of the coal trade with no ready replacement, since steel needs the carbon, not just the heat.
notes.IDN: The largest thermal coal exporter in the world. Jakarta banned exports outright for a month in 2022 to keep its own power stations fed.
notes.RUS: Rerouted from Europe to China and India after 2022, at a discount and over a rail network that was not built for it.
notes.USA: Exports rise whenever European or Asian prices spike, and fall back when they do not — the swing supplier.
notes.COL: Cerrejón is one of the largest open-pit coal mines on earth, and coal is among Colombia's biggest exports after oil.
notes.ZAF: Richards Bay was built to be the largest coal terminal in the world; exports have been throttled for years by the collapse of the state rail line feeding it.
notes.MNG: Coking coal with effectively one customer across one border: China.
notes.CAN: Almost entirely metallurgical coal from British Columbia, shipped to Asian steelmakers.

notes.AUS: The Pilbara. Iron ore is Australia's single largest export by value and the reason its trade balance is so exposed to Chinese construction.
notes.BRA: Carajás produces the highest-grade ore mined anywhere. The Brumadinho dam collapse in 2019 killed 270 people and cut national output for years.
notes.ZAF: Sishen, connected to the coast by an 861km dedicated ore railway.
notes.CAN: Labrador Trough ore, much of it high-grade pellets for European steelmakers.
notes.UKR: Kryvyi Rih sits close to the front line; the mines have kept running through the war.
notes.SWE: Kiruna, above the Arctic Circle. The mine is undermining the town, so the town is being physically moved, building by building.
notes.MRT: Iron ore is most of Mauritania's exports, hauled to the coast on a train two and a half kilometres long.

notes.CAN: Quebec hydro power, and almost all of the metal crosses one border into the United States.
notes.RUS: Rusal is among the largest producers outside China. Western sanctions reshuffled its customers without stopping its output.
notes.ARE: Emirates Global Aluminium runs on gas, which is the Gulf's version of cheap electricity.
notes.IND: Coal-fired smelting, which makes Indian metal the most carbon-intensive of the large exporters.
notes.NOR: Hydro smelters that have been running since the early 1900s, and one of the lowest carbon footprints per tonne anywhere.
notes.ISL: Roughly three quarters of all the electricity Iceland generates goes into aluminium smelting.
notes.BHR: Alba is one of the largest single-site smelters in the world and a substantial share of the Bahraini economy.
notes.MOZ: The Mozal smelter is one of Mozambique's largest exports — a plant built for the power, not the ore.
notes.AUS: Mines the bauxite, refines the alumina, and exports rather less of the finished metal than you would expect.
notes.CHN: By far the largest producer on earth, and it consumes almost all of its own output.

notes.RUS: The largest fertiliser exporter in the world across all three nutrients, and the one input sanctions were repeatedly written to avoid disrupting.
notes.CAN: Saskatchewan sits on the largest potash deposit known, and Canada is the swing supplier of it.
notes.CHN: Has repeatedly restricted phosphate and urea exports outright to hold down prices for its own farmers.
notes.MAR: Holds the overwhelming majority of the world's known phosphate rock — a concentration with no parallel in any other essential mineral.
notes.BLR: One of the top potash exporters until sanctions closed its rail route to Lithuanian ports and left it landlocked.
notes.SAU: Cheap gas turned into urea at scale.
notes.USA: A large exporter and a large importer at once, depending on the nutrient.
notes.EGY: Gas-based urea sold into Europe, which competes for the same gas.
notes.ISR: Potash extracted by evaporating the Dead Sea.
notes.NGA: The Dangote plant turned Nigeria from a fertiliser importer into an exporter in a single step.
notes.QAT: Among the largest urea exporters in the world, on the back of North Field gas.

notes.CHN: The Zhengzhou plant that assembles iPhones can employ 200,000 people in peak season. It is a city built around one product.
notes.VNM: Samsung makes a large share of all its phones here, and is on its own one of Vietnam's biggest exporters.
notes.IND: Went from importing nearly every phone it used to exporting billions of dollars' worth, in about five years, behind tariffs designed to force assembly onshore.
notes.ARE: Dubai is the re-export gateway for handsets moving into Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia.
notes.CZE: A European distribution and configuration hub rather than a factory.
notes.KOR: Designs and sells more phones than it now builds at home.
notes.USA: Designs the highest-value phone in the world and assembles almost none of it.

notes.CHN: Chongqing and Kunshan between them build a large share of the world's laptops.
notes.MEX: Guadalajara assembles for the United States: a day's drive rather than a month at sea.
notes.NLD: A distribution hub. Very little of this was built in the Netherlands.
notes.TWN: The design houses that actually engineer most of the world's laptops are Taiwanese even when the factory is somewhere else.
notes.CZE: Central Europe's assembly and configuration base for the German market.
notes.THA: The world's hard drive industry is concentrated here — which is why the 2011 floods raised storage prices globally.
notes.USA: Servers and high-end systems, where the value is in the design rather than the assembly.
notes.VNM: The fastest-growing alternative to Chinese assembly.

notes.USA: Boeing and a supplier base built over eighty years. Aircraft are consistently among the largest single manufactured exports the United States has.
notes.FRA: Toulouse. Airbus overtook Boeing on deliveries in 2019 and has stayed ahead every year since.
notes.DEU: Hamburg does A320 final assembly and much of the fuselage work.
notes.CAN: Bombardier's regional jet programme ended up inside Airbus; business jets remain a Canadian industry.
notes.GBR: Wings. Broughton in north Wales builds the wings for almost every Airbus flying.
notes.BRA: Embraer is the only manufacturer to have established itself below 150 seats and stayed there.
notes.IRL: Aircraft leasing is an Irish industry: a large share of the world's leased fleet is owned and managed from Dublin, and the aircraft move on Irish paperwork.
notes.ITA: Fuselage sections for Boeing, and ATR turboprops jointly with France.

notes.KOR: Hanwha, HD Hyundai and Samsung. Korea takes most orders for LNG carriers, the most technically demanding ships built.
notes.CHN: Took the volume crown in the 2010s and now leads on container ships and bulk carriers.
notes.JPN: Dominated world shipbuilding until Korea overtook it in the 2000s, and has been slowly ceding ground since.
notes.ITA: Fincantieri builds a large share of the world's cruise ships.
notes.DEU: Meyer Werft, also cruise ships — floated out down a river too narrow for them in a manoeuvre that takes days.
notes.NOR: Specialist offshore, fishing and expedition vessels rather than volume tonnage.
notes.NLD: Dutch yards dominate two odd niches completely: dredgers and superyachts.
notes.TUR: Small and mid-sized vessels, and one of Europe's largest ship recycling industries alongside.
notes.VNM: The low-cost entrant, building hulls for European owners.
notes.FIN: Ice-class ships and icebreakers — a specialism with very few competitors.

notes.CHN: Dominates every step from polysilicon to finished module. The concentration is greater than OPEC ever achieved in oil.
notes.VNM: Assembly capacity built largely by Chinese firms to sit outside American tariffs.
notes.MYS: One of the oldest non-Chinese manufacturing bases, and still one of the largest.
notes.THA: Grew for the same reason as Vietnam, and has been swept into the same tariff investigations.
notes.KHM: A very small economy with a very large solar export line, for the same tariff reason.
notes.DEU: Invented the modern market with its feed-in tariff in 2000, then lost essentially all of the manufacturing to China within a decade.
notes.NLD: A European distribution hub rather than a producer.
notes.IND: Building domestic capacity behind tariff walls, with the explicit aim of not repeating Germany's experience.
notes.USA: Manufacturing is being rebuilt under the Inflation Reduction Act, from a very low base.
notes.KOR: Hanwha Qcells is the last large non-Chinese cell maker with scale.

notes.CHE: The Jura valleys. "Swiss made" is a legally defined label, and it is the reason a movement worth a few hundred francs leaves the country worth thousands.
notes.HKG: The trading and re-export hub for Asia, and a mass-market manufacturing base in its own right.
notes.CHN: Makes most of the world's watches by unit and collects very little of the value — the exact inverse of Switzerland.
notes.FRA: Cartier and the other LVMH and Richemont brands, several of which are made in Switzerland and sold from France.
notes.DEU: Glashütte in Saxony, the one serious continental European alternative to the Swiss, rebuilt after reunification.
notes.JPN: Seiko and Citizen. Japan invented the quartz watch that nearly destroyed the Swiss industry, and now competes with it at the top end too.
notes.SGP: A duty-free re-export point into Southeast Asia.
notes.ARE: Dubai sells to the region and to a very large transiting passenger population.
notes.GBR: Mostly re-export and auction: London remains a centre for the secondary market in fine watches.

notes.USA: The largest services exporter by a wide margin — and the reason the American trade balance is less lopsided than the goods deficit alone suggests. The goods gap gets the attention; the services surplus rarely does.
notes.GBR: Services are what Britain sells. Its surplus on them is among the largest in the world, and it offsets a large part of a persistent goods deficit.
notes.DEU: The mirror image of Britain: a goods powerhouse whose services trade is modest for the size of the economy.
notes.IRL: Fourth in the world from five million people. Software licensing, R&D and royalties booked in Dublin do most of it, which is a tax structure as much as an industry.
notes.FRA: Tourism, transport and business services in roughly equal measure — an unusually balanced services economy.
notes.SGP: Shipping, finance and the regional headquarters of a large share of Asian business, on an island of six million.
notes.IND: Built the largest services export business in the developing world out of IT and back-office work in about thirty years.
notes.CHN: Dominant in goods and comparatively small in services — the exact inverse of the American position.
notes.NLD: Royalties, transport and business services routed through Dutch holding structures.
notes.JPN: Patent income and tourism, from a country whose services exports have grown far slower than its neighbours'.
notes.LUX: Fund administration for the whole of Europe, from a country of 670,000 people.

notes.USA: First, but on an unusual mix: business travel and foreign students. University tuition paid by a non-resident counts here, and American universities collect a great deal of it.
notes.ESP: Second in the world on tourism alone, from a country of 48 million. In a normal year it receives well over 80 million visitors.
notes.FRA: The most visited country on earth by arrivals, but visitors spend less per head than in Spain or the United States, so it earns less than either.
notes.GBR: London does most of it, and the figure has never fully recovered its pre-2016 share.
notes.ARE: Dubai turned a refuelling stop into a destination, and then into one of the most visited cities in the world.
notes.ITA: Art cities and coastline, with the sharpest seasonal concentration of any large destination.
notes.TUR: The fastest-growing large destination of the last decade, helped considerably by a collapsing currency making it cheap.
notes.THA: Tourism was close to a fifth of Thai GDP before 2020, which made the closure of the borders the deepest economic shock in Southeast Asia.
notes.AUS: Education is the larger half — foreign students are Australia's biggest services export.
notes.JPN: A weak yen made Japan abruptly cheap, and visitor numbers hit records the moment it reopened.
notes.MEX: Beach resorts on two coasts, and almost entirely one source market.
notes.SAU: Religious pilgrimage has always been an export; tourist visas for everyone else only arrived in 2019.
notes.CAN: Heavily concentrated on visitors from one neighbour.
notes.HRV: Tourism is a larger share of GDP than in almost any other European country.
notes.GRC: Islands and archaeology, and the sector that carried the economy back out of the debt crisis.

notes.SGP: The busiest transhipment port in the world. Most containers that arrive in Singapore never enter Singapore — they change ship and leave.
notes.DEU: Hapag-Lloyd, and the freight-forwarding industry that organises traffic it does not carry itself.
notes.USA: Air freight and passenger aviation more than sea freight; American carriers are minor in container shipping.
notes.ARE: DP World and Emirates together make Dubai a hub for boxes and for people at the same time.
notes.DNK: Maersk is one of the largest container lines on earth, run from a country of six million.
notes.FRA: CMA CGM, based in Marseille, went from a small line to one of the top three in about twenty years.
notes.CHN: COSCO, plus the sheer volume of freight leaving Chinese ports.
notes.NLD: Rotterdam, Europe's largest port, and the inland barge network behind it.
notes.GBR: Aviation and shipping services rather than ports — Britain's container traffic is modest for its size.
notes.KOR: HMM, rebuilt by the state after the collapse of Hanjin in 2016 left cargo stranded at sea worldwide.
notes.HKG: Once the busiest container port on earth, now well down the list as mainland ports overtook it.
notes.GRC: Greek owners control one of the largest merchant fleets in the world, though the ships mostly fly other countries' flags.
notes.TUR: A land bridge between Europe and Asia, and a large road haulage industry.

notes.USA: Investment banking and asset management. More than a fifth of the world total, and the largest single component of the American services surplus.
notes.GBR: The City. Financial services are Britain's largest export sector and produce its biggest trade surplus with nearly every partner it has.
notes.LUX: 670,000 people, and third in the world. Luxembourg domiciles investment funds for managers based everywhere else in Europe.
notes.DEU: Large banks with a modest cross-border business relative to the size of the economy.
notes.SGP: Asia's fund and wealth management centre, and the main beneficiary of capital and staff leaving Hong Kong since 2020.
notes.FRA: Insurance more than banking — AXA is one of the largest insurers in the world.
notes.IRL: Fund administration, plus the aircraft leasing finance that sits behind the aircraft market.
notes.CHE: Private banking and reinsurance. Swiss Re is one of the two largest reinsurers on earth, and Zurich one of the largest insurers.
notes.HKG: The traditional gateway to Chinese capital markets, now openly competing with Singapore to keep the role.
notes.NLD: Pension funds, among the largest pools of managed capital per head anywhere.
notes.JPN: Vast domestic savings and a comparatively small cross-border financial services business.
notes.CAN: Banks and pension funds; the Canadian pension plans are among the largest institutional investors in the world.

notes.USA: Consulting, software, engineering and R&D, and the deepest bench of professional services firms anywhere.
notes.IRL: Second in the world, from five million people. Software licensed and research booked in Dublin does most of it — an industry and a tax structure in roughly equal parts.
notes.IND: Bangalore, Hyderabad and Pune. India built this out of nothing after 1991 and it now employs over five million people directly.
notes.DEU: Engineering, industrial design and technical consulting — services sold alongside the machinery.
notes.NLD: Royalties and business services routed through Dutch holding structures rather than performed in the Netherlands.
notes.FRA: Consulting and engineering, and a large advertising industry.
notes.CHN: Growing quickly from a low base; software and business process work rather than the licensing that dominates elsewhere.
notes.JPN: Engineering and technical services attached to its manufacturing exports.
notes.GBR: Law, accountancy, advertising and management consulting — the professional services cluster around London.
notes.SGP: Regional headquarters services for companies operating across Southeast Asia.
notes.CHE: Commodity trading and corporate services alongside the pharmaceutical research.
notes.KOR: Engineering and construction design services sold with its industrial exports.
notes.PHL: The largest voice call-centre industry in the world, having taken that segment from India.
notes.ISR: R&D centres operated in Israel by a large share of the world's technology companies.
notes.POL: Europe's near-shored back office — shared service centres for banks and manufacturers across the continent.

notes.USA: Close to a third of the world's licence income: patents, brands, software and the film and television business.
notes.NLD: Second in the world. Dutch holding companies collect royalties for groups headquartered elsewhere, a structure the OECD tax reforms were written specifically to unwind.
notes.JPN: Automotive and electronics patents, plus a large and fast-growing income from games and characters — Nintendo and Pokémon are a measurable share of it.
notes.DEU: Industrial and automotive patents, licensed to manufacturers building German designs elsewhere.
notes.GBR: Pharmaceutical patents, music publishing and television formats, which are exported far more successfully than the programmes themselves.
notes.CHE: Pharmaceutical patents held in a jurisdiction with an unusually favourable regime for taxing income from them.
notes.FRA: Luxury brand licensing as much as technical patents.
notes.SGP: Regional intellectual property holding for Asian operations, for much the same reasons as the Netherlands.
notes.IRL: Software and pharmaceutical licences, on a scale that has repeatedly distorted Irish national accounts.
notes.SWE: Ericsson's mobile telecoms patents. An unusually large share of one small country's IP income comes from the standards inside every phone.
notes.KOR: Samsung and LG patents, and an entertainment export business that barely existed twenty years ago.
notes.CHN: Rising fast from a very low base — for most of the period covered here China paid out far more in licence fees than it collected.

notes.BRA: The largest exporter of leaf in the world, grown mostly on small family farms across the three southern states.
notes.ZWE: Tobacco is Zimbabwe's biggest export by a wide margin, and the crop that came through the land reform upheaval better than any other.
notes.IND: One of the largest producers on earth, and it smokes or chews most of what it grows.
notes.USA: Once the defining American export crop. Ending the federal quota system in 2004 consolidated it into far fewer and much larger farms.
notes.MWI: Among the most tobacco-dependent economies anywhere — it has repeatedly been more than half of Malawi's export earnings.
notes.CHN: The largest producer in the world and barely an exporter: the state monopoly sells to its own enormous domestic market.
notes.BEL: Leaf storage and processing rather than growing.
notes.NLD: Rotterdam is where a great deal of the world's leaf changes hands.
notes.TUR: Oriental tobacco, a distinct sun-cured leaf used for blending rather than on its own.
notes.TZA: One of Africa's fastest-growing producers, largely on Chinese demand.
notes.MOZ: Grown under contract farming schemes that reach a large share of the rural population.

notes.THA: The largest producer and exporter for decades, and unusually it is a smallholder industry rather than a plantation one.
notes.IDN: Second, and the crop that first drew Sumatra into the world economy.
notes.CIV: Africa's largest producer and now among the top few in the world — the crop Côte d'Ivoire pushed hardest to diversify away from cocoa.
notes.VNM: Grown largely on former state farms in the central highlands.
notes.MYS: The country that industrialised rubber after the British brought seedlings from Kew, and now more processor and trader than grower.
notes.BRA: Where the tree comes from. Brazil lost the entire industry to leaf blight and to seeds smuggled to Asia — the Amazon rubber boom ended almost overnight.
notes.LAO: Planted on a large scale with Chinese investment, aimed at Chinese tyre factories.
notes.MMR: A growing producer, hampered by quality and by the political situation.
notes.SGP: The regional trading and pricing centre for a crop it does not grow.
notes.CMR: West and Central Africa's other significant producer.
notes.IND: Kerala grows most of it, and India consumes nearly all of its own crop.

notes.MEX: Michoacán is one of the few places where avocado trees flower year-round, so Mexico can ship every month of the year. The money involved has drawn serious cartel extortion into the orchards.
notes.NLD: Ripening rooms and distribution for the whole of Europe. Not one is grown here.
notes.PER: Counter-seasonal to Mexico, which is precisely why European buyers built the trade.
notes.CHL: The earliest Southern Hemisphere exporter, though water scarcity in Petorca has become a national argument.
notes.ESP: Europe's only significant grower, in Málaga and Granada, and a large re-exporter besides.
notes.ZAF: Ships into Europe in the northern summer gap.
notes.COL: The fastest-growing new origin, on Hass planted at altitude.
notes.KEN: Africa's largest exporter, and increasingly a supplier to China.
notes.ISR: A long-established grower with an unusually high yield per hectare.
notes.DOM: The largest producer of green-skinned varieties, sold mainly into the United States.

notes.AUS: Merino, and the great majority of it goes to China. The national flock is a fraction of what it was before the 1991 collapse of the reserve price scheme.
notes.NZL: Coarse crossbred wool for carpets and insulation — a market synthetic fibre has been eating for fifty years.
notes.ZAF: Fine merino from the Eastern Cape, sold into the same Chinese mills.
notes.GBR: British wool is coarse and cheap; in some years the clip has been worth less than the cost of shearing it.
notes.URY: One of the few economies where wool is still a meaningful share of exports.
notes.ARG: Patagonian merino, on a scale far below its early twentieth-century peak.
notes.FRA: A processing and trading role more than a producing one.
notes.DEU: Scouring and topmaking for the European textile industry.
notes.CZE: A small but persistent wool-processing industry.

notes.CAN: British Columbia spruce-pine-fir, almost all of it to the United States, and the subject of the longest-running trade dispute in North America.
notes.RUS: Banned exports of unprocessed logs in 2022 to force sawmilling onshore; sanctions then closed the European market it had been aiming at.
notes.SWE: Managed boreal forest, planted and cut on a rotation measured in decades and mapped tree by tree.
notes.FIN: Same forest, same model, and an industry that is a far larger share of a smaller economy.
notes.DEU: Bark beetle outbreaks killed so much spruce that Germany briefly became one of the largest exporters in the world, selling salvaged timber.
notes.BRA: Both plantation pine and, more contentiously, tropical hardwood.
notes.CHL: Radiata pine plantations, one of the fastest-growing softwoods anywhere.
notes.AUT: Alpine spruce, and a sawmilling industry that processes far more than Austria grows.
notes.USA: A large exporter and a much larger importer, depending entirely on the housing cycle.
notes.NZL: Radiata pine, most of it shipped as logs to China rather than sawn at home.
notes.LVA: Timber is among the largest export sectors of all three Baltic states.

notes.MDG: The Sava region grows most of the world's vanilla. Cyclone Enawo in 2017 pushed prices past $500 a kilo and brought theft, night patrols and a great many beans picked before they were ready.
notes.IDN: The main alternative origin, and the one buyers turn to whenever Madagascar's price runs away.
notes.PNG: A smallholder crop grown alongside cocoa and coffee.
notes.UGA: Two harvests a year rather than one, which is unusual for the crop.
notes.FRA: Curing, grading and re-export, and the historic link to Réunion where hand-pollination was worked out in 1841.
notes.DEU: Extraction into vanilla flavouring for the food industry.
notes.USA: The largest consumer market, and a substantial re-exporter of extract.
notes.MEX: Where the vanilla orchid comes from, and for centuries the only place it would fruit — its pollinating bee lives nowhere else.
notes.IND: A small producer that expanded during the price spike and largely retreated afterwards.
notes.COM: The Comoros, along with Madagascar and Réunion, make up the historic Indian Ocean vanilla islands.

notes.MEX: Mostly Corona and Modelo crossing a single border. Mexico passed the Netherlands to lead this market in the 2010s and has pulled away since.
notes.NLD: Heineken is brewed in more countries than any other beer, and the Netherlands still exports a great deal of it from home.
notes.BEL: Abbey ales and lambics fetch prices no volume brewer can approach, on a fraction of the litres.
notes.DEU: Enormous production and a stubbornly domestic industry — Germans drink most of what Germany brews.
notes.IRL: Guinness, brewed at St James's Gate and shipped in concentrate to be reconstituted abroad.
notes.CZE: The country that invented pilsner and still drinks more beer per head than anywhere else.
notes.GBR: Ale and stout, and a large contract-brewing business for foreign brands.
notes.FRA: Kronenbourg and a fast-growing craft sector in Alsace and the north.
notes.ESP: One of Europe's largest producers, and almost all of it drunk at home or by visitors.
notes.SGP: A regional distribution point rather than a brewing centre.
notes.POL: Europe's third-largest producer by volume, on very low costs.

notes.ESP: Spain built the biggest pig industry in Europe and was positioned exactly right when Chinese demand spiked after African swine fever.
notes.USA: The lowest-cost large producer, selling into Mexico, Japan and Korea.
notes.DEU: Was Europe's leading exporter until African swine fever in wild boar closed its Asian markets in 2020.
notes.NLD: Slaughter and processing at a scale far beyond Dutch consumption, much of it for re-export.
notes.CAN: Sells into the United States, Japan and China, and imports American piglets to finish.
notes.BRA: The fastest-growing exporter, on cheap feed from its own soy and maize.
notes.DNK: Several times more pigs than people, and an industry organised around export from the beginning.
notes.CHN: The largest producer and the largest importer at once — it eats roughly half the world's pork.
notes.POL: A large producer and an even larger importer of piglets from Denmark and the Netherlands.
notes.FRA: Brittany does most of it, and the industry is a persistent source of water pollution disputes.
notes.BEL: Processing and re-export, and briefly shut out of Asia by its own swine fever outbreak in 2018.
notes.MEX: A growing exporter to Japan even as it remains a huge importer from the United States.

notes.BRA: The largest exporter in the world, and for years the only major producer without a high-pathogenicity bird flu outbreak on a commercial farm.
notes.USA: Exports the dark meat and the feet that Americans will not eat, largely to Asia and West Africa.
notes.NLD: Processing and re-export — the Netherlands trades far more poultry than it raises.
notes.POL: The EU's largest producer, built in about twenty years on costs the west of the union cannot match.
notes.THA: Cooked and processed chicken for Japan and Europe, a niche built deliberately after bird flu closed the raw trade in 2004.
notes.TUR: A large exporter into the Middle East, with an industry that scaled quickly in the 2010s.
notes.UKR: One producer accounts for most of it, and the war cost the industry a large part of its flock.
notes.CHN: Both a major processor of imported meat and an exporter of cooked product.
notes.DEU: Slaughter and processing, with a heavy reliance on imported birds.
notes.BEL: Cutting and re-export for the European market.
notes.HUN: Foie gras and duck as much as chicken — a specialist rather than a volume exporter.

notes.KAZ: Roughly two fifths of world uranium production, almost all by in-situ leaching — pumping solution through the ore body rather than digging it out.
notes.RUS: Mines a modest share and enriches an enormous one. A large part of the West's reactor fuel has passed through Russian centrifuges.
notes.CAN: The Athabasca basin holds the highest-grade uranium ever found, in ore bodies too radioactive to mine by hand.
notes.NAM: Two very large open pits in the Namib desert, mining ore grades a fraction of Canada's.
notes.AUS: Holds the largest reserves in the world and mines cautiously, under state-by-state bans that have only recently loosened.
notes.NER: Niger's uranium supplied French reactors for half a century; the 2023 coup put that arrangement in doubt.
notes.UZB: A steady mid-sized producer that sells mainly east.
notes.FRA: Enrichment and fuel fabrication rather than mining — Orano's plants serve reactors across Europe.
notes.NLD: Urenco's Almelo plant, one of the few enrichment sites outside Russia.
notes.DEU: Fuel fabrication and the transit that comes with it.
notes.GBR: The third leg of Urenco, at Capenhurst.
notes.USA: A large importer of enrichment services and, since the sanctions, in a hurry to rebuild its own.

notes.FRA: Europe's largest exporter in most years, on a nuclear fleet built to run flat out. When those reactors went offline for corrosion checks in 2022, France became a net importer for the first time in decades.
notes.DEU: A large exporter and a large importer at once: the German grid is the crossroads of the European market.
notes.CAN: Quebec and Manitoba hydro, sold south into New England and the upper Midwest.
notes.SWE: Hydro in the north, nuclear in the south, and a persistent surplus.
notes.NOR: Almost entirely hydro, and increasingly a battery for the North Sea wind fleet through undersea cables.
notes.CHE: Buys cheap at night and sells dear at peak — pumped storage run as an export business.
notes.AUT: Alpine hydro and a trading role between Germany and Italy.
notes.LAO: Set out to be the battery of Southeast Asia, damming Mekong tributaries to sell power to Thailand and Vietnam. The debt behind it is a national issue.
notes.PRY: Itaipú and Yacyretá generate several times what Paraguay uses; the surplus goes to Brazil and Argentina under treaties that have been argued over for decades.
notes.CZE: A coal and nuclear surplus sold into Germany and Austria.
notes.BGR: The Balkans' main exporter, on nuclear and lignite.
notes.ESP: Sells into Portugal and, over a famously thin interconnection, into France.

notes.CHN: Produces more steel than everyone else put together. Its exports are a small share of its own output and a very large share of world trade, which is why they are litigated everywhere.
notes.JPN: High-grade sheet for cars and appliances, sold on specification rather than price.
notes.KOR: POSCO, built from nothing in the 1970s with Japanese reparations money and now among the most efficient mills anywhere.
notes.DEU: Specialty and electrical steels, and an industry facing an expensive conversion to hydrogen.
notes.RUS: Sanctioned out of the European market it had supplied for decades, and now selling east at a discount.
notes.IND: Overtook Japan to become the second-largest producer in the world, and unlike China it is still building.
notes.TUR: The largest steelmaker in Europe by output, running almost entirely on imported scrap in electric arc furnaces.
notes.UKR: Mariupol's two enormous mills were destroyed in 2022 and the industry lost most of its capacity.
notes.ITA: Brescia's scrap-based mini-mills, plus Taranto, the largest and most contested blast furnace in Europe.
notes.TWN: China Steel, and a large specialty stainless business.
notes.BEL: Rolling and coating rather than smelting, and a major transit route.
notes.NLD: IJmuiden, one of the last integrated works on the North Sea coast.

notes.ZAF: The Bushveld complex holds the overwhelming majority of world reserves. The mines run several kilometres down, and the industry's modern history runs through the 2012 Marikana killings.
notes.RUS: Palladium more than platinum, produced as a by-product of Norilsk's nickel — which makes its supply hostage to a different market entirely.
notes.GBR: London is where the metal is priced and much of it is vaulted.
notes.CHE: Refining and vaulting, on the same model as its gold business.
notes.ZWE: The Great Dyke is the only other significant primary platinum geology anywhere on earth.
notes.USA: Two mines in Montana, and a large recycling industry pulling metal back out of scrapped catalytic converters.
notes.DEU: Refining and the autocatalyst manufacturing that consumes most of the metal.
notes.JPN: A large importer and refiner, and historically the biggest market for platinum jewellery.
notes.HKG: The route into Chinese jewellery demand.

notes.IDN: Banned ore exports in 2020 and built the smelters instead, mostly with Chinese capital. Indonesia was 2% of this market in 2015 and is around half of it now — step the years and you can watch the policy work.
notes.RUS: Norilsk produces some of the highest-purity class 1 nickel, the grade batteries actually need, from mines inside the Arctic Circle.
notes.CAN: Sudbury has been mined since the 1880s — the crater of an ancient meteorite impact.
notes.AUS: A high-cost producer that has repeatedly mothballed mines when Indonesian supply pushed the price down.
notes.PHL: The main alternative ore supplier to China after Indonesia shut its exports, and the subject of its own mining bans.
notes.NOR: Refines imported ore using cheap hydro power.
notes.FIN: Harjavalta, one of the few refineries in Europe able to make battery-grade nickel.
notes.JPN: Imports ore and exports refined metal, as it does with copper.
notes.CHN: Refines far more than it mines, and owns much of the Indonesian smelting capacity outright.
notes.NCL: New Caledonia sits on a large share of world reserves and has never managed to mine it without political crisis.
notes.BRA: A mid-sized producer with laterite deposits similar to Indonesia's.

notes.CHN: The largest producer and the largest importer at once, and increasingly self-sufficient in the basic polymers it used to buy.
notes.USA: Cheap shale ethane rebuilt the American petrochemical industry along the Gulf Coast after decades of decline.
notes.DEU: Less raw polymer than finished parts, specialty compounds and the machinery to process them.
notes.KOR: A very large refining and petrochemical complex at Yeosu and Daesan, built to export.
notes.BEL: Antwerp is the second-largest petrochemical cluster in the world after Houston.
notes.NLD: Rotterdam's cluster, and the trading that goes with it.
notes.SAU: Cheap ethane — the lowest-cost feedstock there is — turned into polyethylene at Jubail and Yanbu.
notes.JPN: High-value engineering plastics and films rather than commodity resin.
notes.TWN: Formosa Plastics, one of the largest privately held chemical groups anywhere.
notes.ITA: Packaging and machinery, and a large converting industry.
notes.THA: Southeast Asia's petrochemical hub, at Map Ta Phut.
notes.IND: Growing fast, and building refinery-integrated petrochemical capacity at scale.

notes.MMR: Kachin state supplies most of the heavy rare earth ore China separates, from unregulated mines in territory the central government does not control. It is the largest line in this market and the least visible.
notes.CHN: Dominates separation and refining even more thoroughly than mining, and has used export licensing as leverage more than once.
notes.MYS: The Lynas plant at Kuantan is the largest separation facility outside China, and has been fought over locally on waste grounds for more than a decade.
notes.JPN: Built stockpiles, recycling and alternative supply after China cut it off in 2010 — the episode that started every de-risking programme since.
notes.USA: Mountain Pass produces concentrate and has historically shipped it to China to be separated, which is the whole problem in one sentence.
notes.FRA: Solvay's La Rochelle plant, one of the few European separators, running since the 1940s.
notes.EST: Silmet in Sillamäe, a Soviet-era plant that is now part of Europe's small rare earth capacity.
notes.DEU: Magnet manufacturing rather than separation — the step immediately downstream.
notes.IND: Large monazite reserves and very little separation capacity, a gap it is now trying to close.
notes.VNM: Substantial reserves, negligible processing, and repeated false starts at building it.
notes.GBR: Trading and specialist chemicals rather than volume.

notes.NLD: ASML in Veldhoven is the only maker of EUV lithography machines anywhere. On any measure of leverage it is the most consequential company on this map.
notes.JPN: Tokyo Electron, plus Nikon and Canon in older lithography. Japan supplies more of the toolchain than anyone except the Netherlands.
notes.USA: Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA — deposition, etch and inspection rather than lithography, and the origin of most of the export controls.
notes.SGP: Both a manufacturing site for several toolmakers and the regional distribution point.
notes.KOR: Building domestic equipment capacity to reduce its dependence on the same three countries.
notes.TWN: Buys more of this equipment than almost anyone and makes a growing share of the ancillary tooling.
notes.CHN: Buying every tool it is still permitted to buy, and building the ones it is not — with SMEE the most watched company in the country.
notes.DEU: Zeiss makes the optics inside ASML's machines, to tolerances measured in atoms.
notes.AUT: Specialist wafer bonding and lithography for smaller nodes.
notes.MYS: Assembly and test equipment, alongside its packaging industry.

notes.DEU: A dense cluster of small precision manufacturers around Tuttlingen, which has been making surgical instruments since the 1860s.
notes.USA: The largest medtech industry in the world by revenue, though a great deal of its output is manufactured abroad.
notes.NLD: Philips in imaging, plus a substantial distribution role for the European market.
notes.CHN: Moved quickly from disposables into imaging and monitoring equipment, and now competes on price in both.
notes.MEX: Tijuana and Ciudad Juárez assemble much of the disposable device supply for the United States.
notes.IRL: A dozen of the largest device makers manufacture in Ireland, for the same reasons the pharmaceutical industry does.
notes.JPN: Endoscopes above all — Olympus has long held most of that world market.
notes.CHE: Dental and orthopaedic implants, and the machining precision that goes with a watch industry.
notes.BEL: Distribution and repackaging for the EU.
notes.FRA: Diagnostics and imaging, and a large hospital equipment sector.
notes.KOR: Dental imaging and aesthetic devices, growing fast.
notes.SGP: Contract manufacturing for several of the American majors.

notes.CHN: Still the largest by volume by a wide margin, though its share has fallen every year for a decade.
notes.VNM: Nike and Adidas make more shoes in Vietnam than anywhere else on earth, and footwear is among the country's largest exports.
notes.ITA: The value end. Italy exports a small fraction of China's pairs at many times the price per pair.
notes.IDN: The third leg of the athletic industry, and the fallback whenever Vietnamese costs rise.
notes.DEU: Distribution rather than manufacture — the European warehouse for several global brands.
notes.BEL: Antwerp handles a large share of Europe's shoe imports and sends them on.
notes.IND: A very large domestic industry that exports comparatively little, concentrated in Tamil Nadu and Agra.
notes.ESP: Alicante's leather industry, and the volume brands that grew out of it.
notes.PRT: Europe's quiet success story in footwear — high-value, quick-turnaround, and growing.
notes.TUR: Close enough to Europe to restock in days, the same advantage it has in clothing.
notes.KHM: One of the newer low-cost bases, alongside its garment industry.
notes.BRA: Once a major exporter to the United States, now largely serving its own domestic market.

notes.FRA: L'Oréal, LVMH and Chanel. Cosmetics are consistently among France's largest export categories, ahead of most of what it manufactures.
notes.USA: Mass-market beauty at scale, and the largest single consumer market in the world.
notes.DEU: Personal care and household-name mass brands rather than luxury.
notes.SGP: A regional manufacturing and distribution hub for most of the large groups.
notes.KOR: K-beauty went from nothing to a major export in about fifteen years, carried by the same cultural wave as its music and television.
notes.ITA: Contract manufacturing — a large share of the world's lipstick is made in Lombardy for brands that never mention it.
notes.GBR: Fragrance houses and a large retail-driven export trade.
notes.ESP: Puig, plus a substantial fragrance manufacturing base.
notes.IRL: Contract manufacturing and, as everywhere else on this map, booking.
notes.POL: Europe's low-cost contract manufacturing base for cosmetics.
notes.JPN: Skincare above all, and an export business built on the same regional demand Korea competes for.
notes.CHN: Growing fast domestically, and beginning to export brands rather than only ingredients.
